title: Find Median From Data Stream
description:
Implement a `MedianFinder` class that accepts numbers from a stream and reports the median of everything received so far. The median is the middle value of the sorted data, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even.

- `MedianFinder()` creates the object.
- `addNum(num)` adds an integer to the structure.
- `findMedian()` returns the median of all values added so far.
constraints: findMedian is only called after at least one addNum
hints: Keeping a sorted list makes the median trivial to read, but what does each insertion cost? Re-sorting every query is far worse.
The median only depends on the middle one or two elements. Could you split the data into a lower half and an upper half and only look at the boundary?

Use a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. Keep their sizes equal (or lower half one bigger) by rebalancing after each add. The median is the top of the larger heap or the average of both tops.

args.$py: [[]] + [y for i in range(30000) for y in ([i], [])]

expected.$py: [None] + [y for i in range(30000) for y in (None, i / 2)]

args.$py: [[]] + [y for i in range(30000) for y in ([29999 - i], [])]

expected.$py: [None] + [y for i in range(30000) for y in (None, (30000 - (i + 1) + 29999) / 2)]

solution.explanation: Maintain two heaps: a max-heap `small` for the lower half and a min-heap `large` for the upper half. On each add, push into `small`, move its largest to `large`, and if `large` ends up bigger, move its smallest back, so `small` is never smaller than `large` and exceeds it by at most one. The median is the top of `small` for an odd count, or the average of both tops for an even count. Adds cost O(log n), median queries O(1), memory O(n).
